body:
### Summary

`npm test` is nondeterministic on CI. It blocked the 1.67.0 npm publish: the release job created the tag and GitHub Release, then the `publish` job's `npm test` failed with 12 unrelated failures, so `npm publish` never ran. 1.67.0 was live everywhere except npm until the job was re-run.

### Evidence it's flaky, not a regression

A different, non-overlapping set of tests fails on each run of `main`:

| Commit | Failing tests |
|---|---|
| `ce7a9dc8` | SDK concurrency limiter, Error classification Retry-After (5), Empty messages array, Passthrough streaming/non-streaming tool_use |
| `d406404f` | Stale UUID retry, OpenCode title agent, graceful shutdown, Session lineage pruning, Extra usage fallback |
| earlier | Rate-limit retry backoff, Plugin integration e2e, MCP server per-request lifecycle |

The failures span concurrency, plugins, MCP, sessions, and error classification — no common subsystem. The same commit content passed CI on `6c85fcd5` and failed on `ce7a9dc8`, where the only diff is the version bump and changelog. The full suite passes locally (exit 0).

Recent `main` CI conclusions: `ce7a9dc8` fail, `6c85fcd5` pass, `d406404f` fail, `85d18d9c` pass, `1ea97d01` pass, `3ff4c0a5` pass, `0f38de84` pass, `00a2f82d` fail — roughly a 1-in-3 failure rate.

Note `d406404f` is #931 ("give every file its own module mocks instead of racing for one"), which was intended to address cross-file mock leakage and itself failed CI on `main`. So whatever remains is not fixed by per-file mocks alone.

Several failures are timing-shaped (`this test timed out after 5000ms`), suggesting runner contention or real cross-test interference rather than pure mock leakage.

### Why it matters

Releases are gated on this suite. A flaky gate on the publish step produces exactly the partial state seen here — tag and GitHub Release created, npm not published — which is silent unless someone checks `npm view`. It also trains contributors to dismiss red CI, which is how a real failure gets waved through (see the #921 PR body, where a contributor reported `proxy-stale-uuid-retry.test.ts` failing on a clean `origin/main` worktree and reasonably assumed it was pre-existing).

### Suggested directions

- Identify whether failures are ordering-dependent (does `--randomize` / a fixed seed reproduce them?)
- Look for shared process-global state beyond `mock.module` — module-level caches, timers, the session store, env vars
- Consider raising or removing the 5s timeouts on the tests that time out, if they're genuinely slow rather than hung
- Consider making the `publish` job's gate the already-green `main` CI run for the same tree, rather than a fresh `npm test` execution that re-rolls the dice

## Investigation update — reproduced locally, root cause narrowed, not yet fixed

### Correction to the original report

I suggested gating the publish job on the already-green `main` CI run for the same tree. **That wouldn't have worked** — CI *also* failed on `ce7a9dc8`, the release commit. There was no green run to gate on. Scratch that suggestion.

### Reproduced locally

3× the main pass (macOS, under CPU contention):

| run | result |
|---|---|
| 1 | 3028 pass / 0 fail |
| 2 | **1 fail** — `Integration: Concurrent subagent requests > should handle 3 concurrent requests` |
| 3 | 3028 pass / 0 fail |

So it is not CI-specific. Roughly matches the ~1-in-3 CI rate.

### It is cross-file, not within-file

- `integration.test.ts` alone: **0 failures in 15 runs**
- The two files owning the recurring cluster, run together: **0 failures in 10 runs**
- Both fail only inside the full suite

That is the #917 signature quoted in `sdkMock.ts`: *"nothing reproducing when a file runs on its own."*

### There is a stable recurring cluster

`ce7a9dc8` (CI) and #936 (CI) failed with the **same 11 tests**, from exactly two files:

- `proxy-error-handling.test.ts` — Retry-After (#901) ×5, Empty messages array (#450) ×1
- `proxy-passthrough-tool-use.test.ts` — Passthrough streaming ×3, non-streaming ×2

Only *part* of each file fails, so it isn't whole-file replacement.

### Mechanism the evidence points at

`src/__tests__/sdkMock.ts` keeps a single module-global:

```ts
let active: SdkMockModule | null = null
```

`installSdkMock(factory)` registers a `beforeAll` that assigns `active = factory()`. It is never reset on `afterAll`, and correctness rests on one documented premise:

> Because bun runs files sequentially, exactly one implementation is ever active.

The failing tests set a module-level `mockError`, issue a request, and expect an error status. Their failure mode is receiving a **success** — i.e. `active` was some *other* file's implementation at the moment they ran. That is what the single-global design produces if the sequential premise is violated at scale (file-level parallelism, or an in-flight async request from a previous file resolving after the next file's `beforeAll` has swapped `active`).

Note the second path does not require bun parallelism at all: any request not fully awaited when a file ends will resolve against the *next* file's implementation.

### Not verified yet

- Whether bun is actually running files concurrently here, or whether the leak is purely un-awaited async work crossing a file boundary. A timestamp-instrumented pair of files would distinguish these.
- Why this specific cluster is the frequent victim.

### Directions

- Reset `active = null` in an `afterAll` inside `installSdkMock`. `resolve()` already throws a named error when nothing is installed, so a leaked call becomes a **loud, attributable failure at its true origin** instead of a silent wrong-mock success in a later file. Diagnostic even if it doesn't fix the cause.
- Have `resolve()` compare `activeOwner` against the file whose test is running and throw on mismatch — turns the silent corruption into a precise report of who leaked into whom.
- Audit the two victim files (and `integration.test.ts`) for requests that aren't awaited before the test ends.

I stopped short of shipping a fix: without a reliable reproduction, any change here is unfalsifiable, and a wrong "fix" to a flaky suite is worse than a documented one. The `afterAll` reset above is the smallest defensible next step and is mostly diagnostic.

## Update 2 — one real finding, one rejected fix, and a correction

### Correction: this is not (only) flakiness — `main` fails deterministically on CI

Re-running CI on `ce7a9dc8` (unchanged tree, none of #936's code) reproduced **the identical 11 failures**, twice. PR #936 also failed twice with the same 11. So for a given tree the failure set is deterministic on Linux CI, while the same tree passes on macOS. `6c85fcd5` passed, so it is tree-dependent rather than permanent — matching the #917 note that the set is "stable for a given file set."

The 11 come from exactly two files:

- `proxy-error-handling.test.ts` — Retry-After ×5, Empty messages ×1
- `proxy-passthrough-tool-use.test.ts` — Passthrough streaming ×3, non-streaming ×2

### Correction: they fail with 500, not with a bogus success

My first comment guessed the tests were receiving successes (wrong-mock). The CI log shows otherwise — they expect 429/503/402 and receive **500**. `mockError` *is* firing; the status is just not the classified one. So a plain wrong-mock swap does not fit.

### Real finding: one of the two files pays ~12s of real backoff sleeps

The proxy sleeps `RATE_LIMIT_BASE_DELAY_MS * 2^(attempt-1)` between rate-limit retries — a real 1000ms then 2000ms. The CI log shows it:

```
[PROXY] 3aa7fdfc rate-limited on sonnet, retry 1/2 in 1000ms
(fail) ... puts a conservative hint on a 429 [1026.99ms]
```

Measured locally on `proxy-error-handling.test.ts`:

| setting | runtime (18 tests) |
|---|---|
| default (1000ms base) | 13.46s / 13.75s |
| `MERIDIAN_RATE_LIMIT_BASE_DELAY_MS=1` | 1.52s / 1.60s |

Three real seconds inside bun's 5000ms per-test budget is comfortable on a fast machine and marginal on a loaded 2-core runner. That is a plausible mechanism for this file's 6 failures and for the `timed out after 5000ms` failures seen on other runs.

### Rejected fix: do NOT set it globally in the preload

The obvious fix — `process.env.MERIDIAN_RATE_LIMIT_BASE_DELAY_MS ??= "1"` in `src/__tests__/preload.ts` — **regresses `priority-routing-integration.test.ts`**:

| preload override | result (3 runs) |
|---|---|
| with | 1 fail, 2 fail, 1 fail |
| without | 0 fail, 0 fail, 0 fail |

`keyless priority affinity > gives two keyless conversations independent assignments` depends on the real delay. A global override trades an intermittent failure for a deterministic one. Reverted, not shipped.

### What this does not explain

`proxy-passthrough-tool-use.test.ts` runs in **426ms** and pays no backoff cost, yet owns 5 of the 11 failures. So the backoff is at most half the story. Either there are two causes, or a common one upstream of both that I have not found.

### Suggested next steps

- Scope the delay override to `proxy-error-handling.test.ts` only (the pattern `proxy-rate-limit-retry.test.ts` already uses), rather than globally. Removes ~12s from the main pass and the timeout pressure on those 6 tests, with no effect on the priority-routing file.
- Investigate the passthrough 5 separately — they are fast, so timeouts are not the mechanism there.
- Because it is deterministic per tree on Linux, a CI run with `--reporter=verbose` on `ce7a9dc8` (or a Linux container locally) should be enough to see the real error body behind the 500s, which is the fastest way to settle the passthrough half.

Two of these are diagnosed and fixed on main (`d3bfe795`, #986). Both were
**time-budget expiries, not logic failures**, and both appeared on diffs that
could not have affected them — which is what made them clean observations:

```
windows-smoke   process-incarnation.test.ts:123    10265 ms
test            failover-request-id.test.ts:76     5002.97 ms
```

@justprosh hit the second one independently while working on #966 and pushed an
empty commit to retrigger, so that is a second sighting rather than a
coincidence.

**Measured rather than guessed.** `failover-request-id` runs **4.05 s locally
against bun's 5 s default** — under a second of margin, which a contended runner
eats. 5002.97 ms is the default boundary to the millisecond, not an assertion
failing. It drives a full priority-failover round trip through the HTTP layer, so
it is legitimately slow rather than stuck: the budget was wrong. Now 30 s.

I also scanned every test file doing real I/O without an explicit timeout, since
"which tests run closest to their budget" is the useful question here:

```
launcher-script                      2.01 s
passthrough-early-stop-integration   6.15 s   (81 tests, ~76 ms each)
everything else                      < 1 s
```

No other single test is near the default.

The Windows one is a different bug and not a budget change. The probe has its
own 10 s subprocess budget; when it expired the module did what it is designed
to do — failed closed and returned `undefined` — while the test demanded
success. It now retries, and the strict assertion is kept: a capture that never
succeeds across three attempts is a real defect, and loosening it to "defined or
undefined" would assert nothing.

**Leaving both issues open.** Neither of these is a concurrency test, and this
issue is specifically about concurrency tests failing fast and never the same one
twice. Widening timeouts across the suite would quiet CI and mask exactly that,
so only the one test with a measured sub-second margin was touched. Whether the
concurrency suite has its own distinct cause is still open.

**Correction to my previous comment**, plus two more sightings fixed (#990,
`92698147`).

I claimed a scan had found no other test near the 5s default. **That scan was
too narrow** — it filtered to files mentioning `startProxyServer` / `spawnSync`
/ `createProxyServer`, so it never examined `session-lineage.test.ts`, which
drives HTTP through a local `createTestApp()` helper. Two more expiries then
appeared on a docs-only PR:

```
session-lineage.test.ts        "second compaction ..."      5317.03 ms
proxy-extra-usage-fallback     "does not use ... backoff"    756.01 ms
```

Rescanned across **every** test file this time. File totals over 2s:

```
106.16s  priority-routing-integration   (72 tests, 48 already annotated)
 19.86s  error-telemetry-profile        (5 tests, 1 annotated)
 13.98s  proxy-error-handling           (19 tests, 1 annotated)
  7.60s  passthrough-early-stop-integration
  7.52s  proxy-cross-process-coordination
  6.59s  proxy-concurrency-coordination
```

`error-telemetry-profile` averages ~4s per test against a 5s default. Annotating
tests one at a time as they fail is whack-a-mole, so the harness budget is now
30s for the whole suite (`bun test --timeout 30000`). A hung test still fails;
only legitimately-slow ones stop being killed.

**Why that is not the "widen timeouts to quiet CI" move I warned against**, since
it looks like exactly that: this issue describes concurrency tests that **fail
fast** — quick assertion failures, not timeouts. A longer default cannot hide
them, because they never reach the budget.

The backoff test needed a different fix. It asserted wall-clock `elapsed < 500`
against a real backoff floor of 1000ms and failed at **756ms — below the
floor**, so no backoff had happened and the assertion was measuring a contended
runner. Nudging the bound to 1000 would only relocate the coin-flip, so the
signal is amplified instead: `MERIDIAN_RATE_LIMIT_BASE_DELAY_MS=10000` makes a
single backoff cost 10s, which no runner noise can imitate.

Still leaving this open. Every failure diagnosed so far has been a timeout or a
wall-clock assertion, and none has been a concurrency test. Whether the
concurrency suite has its own distinct cause is unanswered, and that is what
this issue is actually about.

A new concrete CI timeout was addressed without weakening its assertion. On the 2026-09-26 `main` [Windows smoke run](https://github.com/rynfar/meridian/actions/runs/36222500658/job/108350267134), the working-directory HTTP test exceeded Bun's 5-second default at 5,313 ms even though its mocked response completed. The same assertion passed in 141 ms on the later release run. [#1162](https://github.com/rynfar/meridian/pull/1162) scopes the existing 30-second main-suite bound to the three Windows CWD files; the exact Windows gate, full `test`, and other final-head checks passed before merge.

This is one measured timeout path. It does not explain the original fast assertion failures or prove that all `npm test` flakiness is gone, so #933 remains open for those observations.

title: npm test is flaky on CI (~1 in 3 runs) and blocked the 1.67.0 npm publish
